conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I understand you came in with right upper quadrant pain and vomiting. Can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, thank you. I’ve had Crohn’s for years and usually get pain on the left side, but this time it’s sharp and in the upper right, near my back. Started about five days ago after I ate a hamburger on vacation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you’ve had nausea and vomiting—was it bile-colored?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, greenish. I’ve vomited a few times. I haven’t passed gas in days and my last bowel movement had blood in the toilet, not in the stool. That’s unusual—I’m usually loose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s important. Your history of multiple bowel surgeries makes us concerned about obstruction. You mentioned placing your own NG tube at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve done it before when I feel blocked. It helps. I did it again after the ED removed mine—didn’t know why they took it out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep it in for now to help decompress your stomach. We’ve ordered blood work and a CT scan to check for obstruction or other causes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m worried it’s another blockage. But this pain feels different—more constant and deeper.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re looking into that. Given your history, we’re also checking liver and gallbladder, even though you’ve had your gallbladder out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows the NG tube is in place. We’re waiting on the CT results. Any change in pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still hurting, but the tube helps a little. I’m anxious—being in the hospital brings back bad memories.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. We’ve noted your PTSD history. We’ll be cautious with medications. Let’s wait for the CT before increasing anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The CT scan is back. Good news—no bowel obstruction, no inflammation or perforation. But we see mild fatty liver and a stable adrenal nodule.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No blockage? But I feel blocked. My belly is distended and I haven’t moved my bowels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The scan shows gas in the colon, but no mechanical obstruction. It might be a functional slowdown—common in Crohn’s with adhesions. We’ll keep the NG tube and start bowel stimulants.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Can I try coffee? It’s helped before with motility.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can try a small amount once we confirm your electrolytes are stable. We’re also checking for infection—your labs show no signs of inflammation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal X-ray shows dilated bowel loops, likely due to a known stricture. But no free air, so no perforation. We’ll give an enema to help with constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. The pain is still bad. Can I have something stronger for pain? I know I’ve had Dilaudid before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We can give IV Dilaudid, but we need to be cautious. You’re on Valium at home, and combining them increases sedation risk. We’ll monitor you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But the pain is overwhelming. I trust you to keep me safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You passed stool last night after the enema and coffee. That’s progress. Your pain seems a bit better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a little. But I still need pain meds. Can I have the Dilaudid again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave a dose last night. We’re concerned because your oxygen dipped briefly after—likely due to the combination with Valium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember—I felt like I stopped breathing for a second. That scared me. It brought back trauma from a past hospital stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A rapid response was called, and you responded well to Narcan. No lasting effects. But we need to be very careful. We’ll adjust your pain plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that. But I still hurt. What are my options?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue low-dose Dilaudid with longer intervals and avoid Valium for now. We’ve also consulted your gastroenterologist and surgeon—they agree with our approach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat chest X-ray shows no pneumonia or fluid. The hypoxia was likely due to sedation, not aspiration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried I’d damaged my lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also watching your EKG. You were on cipro and Zofran, which can prolong the QT interval. Your QT was over 550, so we gave IV magnesium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that before. It runs in my family. Is it better now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s improved to about 440. We’ve stopped the QT-prolonging meds. Please follow up with an EKG as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing better. You passed gas, your abdomen is less distended, and you’re tolerating sips. We’ll try advancing your diet slowly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Can we remove the NG tube soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll try a trial without it today. If you don’t vomit and keep food down, we can remove it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great job—you kept the liquids down. We’re removing the NG tube. How’s the pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. Still there, but manageable. What about pain meds at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll prescribe oral Dilaudid 4 mg every six hours as needed. But no Tramadol—you should avoid it. We’ve coordinated with your PCP and gastroenterologist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember—Dr. ___ said it could trigger seizures with my history. Thank you for checking.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll also continue your gabapentin and other home meds. Your urine had blood initially, but it’s cleared. Still, follow up with a repeat urinalysis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my iron? I’ve been anemic before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your hemoglobin dropped to 9.6, but it’s above your baseline. Continue your iron and vitamin B12. Check labs at your next visit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home today. You’re walking well, eating, and pain is controlled with oral meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. Can my husband come in? I want him to hear the instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. We’ll go over everything. You’re on Dilaudid for pain, but use it sparingly. Avoid driving. Continue all other medications, including fondaparinux for your stent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Follow up with your gastroenterologist and PCP. Get an EKG soon and repeat urinalysis. If pain worsens or you can’t keep food down, return immediately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I feel anxious or PTSD symptoms flare?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Contact your mental health provider. We’ve noted your needs—social work can help coordinate. You’re strong, and we’re here to support you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I’m grateful for your care and patience.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I worry about the adrenal nodule?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s stable and likely benign. Your endocrinologist can monitor it. No action needed now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the liver? The ultrasound said fatty liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mild steatosis. Continue healthy diet and avoid alcohol. It’s common and often stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And my spleen is enlarged?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mild splenomegaly, likely from chronic inflammation. No intervention needed, but your doctor will keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. We’re glad you’re feeling better. Discharge papers are ready—nurse will go over them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to follow up with all my doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the best plan. Take care, and feel better soon.
